transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Yeah, um… I guess what brings me in is what happened at work. I’m a personal care aide, so we have these staff meetings where they go over safety stuff, and there was talk about fall prevention, like making sure people don’t trip, keeping chairs out of the way, how to catch things early.

And I don’t know, I got really worked up in the meeting. Like I felt like I needed to show everybody what I meant, not just say it. So I started moving the chairs around and acting out this whole fall-prevention drill, waving my arms around, kind of demonstrating where someone might fall and how we should respond. It got bigger than I meant it to, honestly. People were telling me to sit down, and I heard them, but I couldn’t seem to stop right away. I just kept going like I had to finish the whole thing.

It was embarrassing afterward, because it wasn’t like a planned presentation or anything. I was just… acting it out in front of everyone, and I could tell folks were uncomfortable. That’s why I’m here.
While you were moving the chairs and acting out the drill, did you feel like you had to do it even though you knew others might not agree or thought it wasn’t the right time?

Yeah… yeah, I think so. At the time, part of me knew it wasn’t the right moment. Like, it was a regular staff meeting, not some training where I was supposed to get up and demonstrate. People were saying, “Sit down,” or trying to get me to stop, and I did hear them. I wasn’t completely unaware of what was happening.

But I felt like I had to finish it, like if I didn’t show the whole thing with the chairs and where somebody might fall and how we should move, then nobody would really understand what I meant. I got so worked up that just explaining it didn’t feel like enough. My arms were going, I was moving chairs around, and even when I could tell people were uncomfortable, I couldn’t seem to shut it off right away. It was like I had started something and my body and my mouth were ahead of me, and stopping felt almost impossible in that moment.
Before you started moving the chairs and acting it out, did you feel a growing sense of tension or pressure inside that you had to do something about?

Yeah… I think there was, like, a buildup. It wasn’t just all of a sudden from calm to moving furniture. I remember sitting there listening to them talk about fall prevention, and I started feeling this pressure in me, like I needed to jump in and show what I meant, not just say it.

At first I was just thinking it through in my head, like, “No, the chair should be over here,” or “This is how somebody could trip,” and then it kind of kept building. My body felt keyed up, like I couldn’t just sit there with my hands still. I felt like if I didn’t do something right then, nobody was going to understand the point I was trying to make.

So, yeah, before I got up and started moving the chairs and waving my arms around, there was definitely this… pressure, I guess. Like an urge to act it out. And once I started, it was hard to stop, even when people were telling me to sit down.
While you were moving the chairs and acting out the drill, did you feel like you were in touch with reality, or did things feel somehow unreal or disconnected?

Um… I’m not totally sure how to answer that. I mean, I knew I was at work. I knew it was the staff meeting, and I knew the people in the room were my coworkers. It didn’t feel like I was somewhere else or dreaming, exactly.

But I was so keyed up and focused on what I was doing that everything else kind of got pushed back, if that makes sense. Like I could hear people telling me to sit down, and I could see their faces, but it was like the main thing in my head was, “No, I have to finish showing this.” So I don’t know if I’d call that disconnected from reality. It felt real. Maybe too real in the moment, like it mattered more than it probably did.

I guess I didn’t feel unreal, but I also wasn’t taking in the room the way I normally would. I was kind of locked into the demonstration.
In the days leading up to that staff meeting, did you notice any changes in your sleep — like needing less sleep than usual or having trouble winding down at night?

Yeah… yeah, that was happening. I wasn’t really seeing it as a problem at the time, though. Like, I could sleep maybe two or three hours, and then I’d be up before dawn, wide awake, like my body was saying, “Okay, we’re done sleeping now.”

And it wasn’t like I woke up and thought, “Oh no, I didn’t sleep enough.” I’d get up while the house was still dark and start thinking through plans, like what needed to happen or how things should be organized. My mind would already be going, and I felt ready to start the day way earlier than normal.

At night, too, it was hard to wind down because I didn’t really feel tired in the usual way. I’d lie there but my head would still be active, and then even if I did fall asleep, I’d pop back up after a couple hours like that was enough. At the time I thought, well, maybe I’m just being productive, you know? I didn’t really think anything was wrong with being up making plans before anyone else was even awake.
Did you feel like you needed less sleep than usual in the days leading up to the meeting?

Yeah, I did. I mean, looking back, yes, I was definitely sleeping less than I normally would, but at the time it didn’t feel like “oh, I’m not sleeping enough.” It felt more like I just didn’t need it.

I’d sleep maybe two or three hours, and then I’d wake up before dawn, like while the house was still dark, and I’d feel ready to get going. Not groggy, not thinking I should go back to bed. My head would already be moving into plans and what needed to be done, and I’d just get up and start thinking things through.

And I didn’t really see anything wrong with it then. I kind of thought, well, I’m up, I’m alert, I might as well use the time. It didn’t feel strange until later, when I looked back and realized most people don’t just pop up after a couple hours of sleep feeling like that’s enough.
